chapter: Jazz at the Philharmonic and the record business
title: Was JATP taped? Asch and Granz
summary: McGhee insists the early JATP concerts were taped rather than put on disk.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: Let's see, that was made in '46. But we did... We never knew when Norman was making these...
I think he taped most of... Not taped in those days...
Yeah, he had them taped or taped them. Because he did the one here at Carnegie Hall!
They cut them on disks, I think.
Well, no, I think they were taping them.
Well, whatever it was, I think most concerts he got down. Most of the time...
Well, even the first one, the first Jazz At The Philharmonic was put on tape. That wasn't for no disk.

No. That was on tape. I was trying to make a point... I made seven dates with him, and I never knew when he was (?), because he had those machines running back there, and you never knew what was going on. There wasn't no disks being made, though. That much I knew. Because I was checkin' that shit out. I said, "Well, I'll see what's happening so I can put my demands in front." But it must have been on tape, because there wasn't no disks being made.
Asch told me that Norman brought in a tape for him to hear, and that's why he was interested in putting it out --
because he heard the whole thing, you know. And you couldn't do that with no disk. You couldn't put all that on a disk. It had to be on a tape.
